packet.prompt:
Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

text:
PACKET-15 - unverified image reading

Exposure statement: Nothing in my context revealed a proposed identification or an
earlier reading of this fragment. Beyond the rules, I made enlarged, contrast-
enhanced crops of packet tiles (stitching adjacent overlapping tiles) in a private
scratch folder. No other source was opened. Several words below look like familiar
scriptural phrasing; I have transcribed only visible letters and marked where a
word is cut off rather than completing it.

=====================================================================
LAYOUT SURVEY
=====================================================================
A narrow strip of parchment (about 24 x 8 cm on the scale), folded along its
long axis and with cut corners: clearly a reused binding strip. Two faces:
- Face 1: overview image-001, tiles image-002 (left), image-003 (centre),
  image-004 (right). Pencil shelf note "Stams, STA, Frg. 17r(?)" (image-002).
  A later blue ink/pencil note, written upside down relative to the text, in the
  lower centre (image-003): approx. "#t/ x(?) [IX?] / Entxmonnicon(?)"
  - not part of the medieval text; I cannot read it securely.
- Face 2: overview image-005, tiles image-006 (left), image-007 (centre),
  image-008 (right). Pencil shelf note "Stams, STA, Frg. 17v" (image-008).

Only the bottom two lines of a single text block survive on each face, written
across the full width of the strip (long lines, no column division visible on
what survives). Script: a formal Gothic textualis, medium size, dark brown ink,
ruled in drypoint/plummet with visible bounding lines. Red is used for a versicle
sign and for touching capitals: on face 1, a red stroke through the capital "V"
(image-003 / image-004); on face 2, a red versicle symbol (a crossed "V", i.e. the
sign for versus/versiculus) followed by a capital "C" touched in red (image-007,
image-008), and the initial "E(?)" at the start of line 2 touched in red
(image-006).

Below the text on face 2 (image-006, image-007, image-008) there are added
musical notes on hand-drawn staves (five-line staves, ruled roughly, with bar-like
vertical strokes): void (hollow) lozenge/oval notes with stems, some black notes,
a C-clef-like sign at the left (image-006) and a large looped sign at the right
end (image-008). The notes are in a different, lighter ink and run over the fold;
tentatively a later addition (pen trial or music added in the blank lower
margin), not part of the main text. Nothing similar on face 1.

Tentative interpretation (observation-based only): a liturgical book with
versicles marked by the red versicle sign; the text lines are prose with
scriptural-sounding wording. No lemma/commentary distinction.

=====================================================================
TRANSCRIPTION
=====================================================================
Conventions: (x) = expansion; word? = uncertain; [...] = lost/cut off;
[illegible]. Line numbers from the top of each image. The same two lines appear
in all three tiles of each face; I give the continuous reading once, noting which
tile each part comes from. Overlaps are not counted as extra text.

FACE 1
image-002 l.1  [...folded corner...] [.]neme(?)                 (left tile; partly
               on the curled corner, distorted)
image-003 l.1  [...]neme(?) erebat(?) & p(re)dicabat dicens. Ven[...]
image-004 l.1  [...]ns. Veniet(?) fort[...]                         (V touched red;
               last word cut by the cut-off upper right corner; I see "fora"/"fort")
image-002 l.2  [.]...me(?) cuius
image-003 l.2  [...]e cuius no(n) sum dignus p(ro)cumbens sol[...]
image-004 l.2  [...]bens solue(re)(?) corri[...]                    ("solue" with a
               superscript abbreviation stroke; final visible letters "corri"/"cori",
               then a hairline; text then lost at the cut)

Combined face 1 (as visible):
  l.1  [...]neme(?) erebat(?) & p(re)dicabat dicens. Veniet(?) fort[...]
  l.2  [...]me(?) cuius no(n) sum dignus p(ro)cumbens solue(re)(?) corri[...]
Note: the first visible word of l.1 is damaged by the folded corner; letters
"..eme" or "..eine" then "erebat"/"ecebat" - I am not certain of the second word.
Line 1 also seems to begin before the left tile's visible area (cut off).

FACE 2
image-006 l.1  pace in credend[o]...
image-007 l.1  [...]n credendo . ut habundetis in spe & uirtu[te](?) ...
image-008 l.1  [...]e & uirtu[...]                                  (cut at the edge;
               "uirtu" is partly lost; the following letters are not visible)
image-006 l.2  E(?)x syon sp(eci)es decoris
image-007 l.2  [...]n sp(eci)es decoris eius d(eu)s manifeste ueniet. [red versicle sign]
image-008 l.2  [...]et. [red versicle sign] Congregate ill[...]     ("Congregate" with
               red-touched C; next word only "ill"/"illi" visible before the break)

Combined face 2 (as visible):
  l.1  pace in credendo . ut habundetis in spe & uirtu[...]
  l.2  E(?)x syon sp(eci)es decoris eius d(eu)s manifeste ueniet. V(ersus) Congregate ill[...]
Notes: "sp(eci)es" is written "spes" with an abbreviation stroke over it.
"d(eu)s" is "ds" with a stroke. The capital at the start of l.2 (image-006) is a
decorated E- or C-like form with red infill; I read "Ex" but the first letter is
not certain.

Added music (face 2, image-006..008): staff(s) with notes only; no text underlay
visible; not transcribed as text. The marks at image-008 right ("Cl" loops and
"a y d" -like strokes on a vertical axis) look like further pen trials, possibly
letters written sideways; illegible to me.

=====================================================================
LIMITATIONS
=====================================================================
- Only two text lines per face survive; the rest of each leaf is cut away. The
  strip's top edge cuts through the ascenders of line 1 on both faces, and the
  cut corners remove the line-ends and line-beginnings.
- The rest of the strip (below the text) is blank on face 1 and carries only the
  added music on face 2; the lower part is a folded turn-in.
- Which face precedes which in the original book cannot be determined from these
  images; the shelf-mark notes say r/v but that is the modern foliation.
- A raking-light or unfolded image of the upper fold and the curled left corner on
  face 1 (image-002) might recover the first word of line 1.
